Statutory framing
Per Michigan School Code Section 380.624(2), the proposed General Fund budget must be submitted to constituent boards for review by May 1, and each constituent board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support no later than June 1. Oakland Schools supplies all fund budgets for review, but constituent districts vote only on the General Fund.

Revenue
Oakland Schools is primarily property-tax funded; the budget projects 3.4% growth in property tax revenue, described as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable value projections since actual figures were unavailable at preparation.

PA-18 special education
Base distribution to local districts is budgeted to increase approximately $5.2 million, or 2.9%. A further $2.5 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursement for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup, extraordinary expenditures and capital. $5.0 million is budgeted to construct an Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Center Program in Oxford. Other items
Over $1.4 million in subsidies for CTE and curriculum/assessment software and instructional tools. Personnel costs include step increases plus a 2.0% salary increase for all staff, subject to collective bargaining.

Key dates
April 17, 2026 presentation to the 28 local business managers; April 29 Designates Meeting at 6:00 PM; June 1 Truth in Budgeting hearing and board consideration.

Agenda item 8.A. at the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 24, 2026 — the full resolution requesting a regional enhancement millage election, with the ballot proposal attached as Exhibit A.

- Estimated to raise $125,756,247 if approved and first levied in 2026
- Distributed on an equal per-pupil basis to local districts and eligible public school academies within Oakland Schools' boundaries

The Superintendent is directed to deliver a certified copy to the Oakland Schools Board Secretary.

This is the complete resolution filed as agenda item 8.A. at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting held February 24, 2026 at 7:00 p.m., captioned "RESOLUTION REQUESTING REGIONAL ENHANCEMENT MILLAGE ELECTION." It is the formal instrument by which Troy asks Oakland Schools Intermediate School District to put a regional enhancement millage before voters, and it carries the proposed ballot language as Exhibit A.

The preamble sets out the statutory mechanism in four WHEREAS clauses. Section 705 of the Revised School Code of 1976 as amended (MCL 380.705) provides for the levy of a regional enhancement property tax by an intermediate school district at a rate not to exceed 3 mills, for the purpose of enhancing other state and local funding for local school operating purposes, if approved by a majority of the ISD electors. Proceeds are paid to each constituent school district — including eligible public school academies — by the ISD in an amount calculated on a per-pupil basis. A constituent district may request the ISD to submit the question to voters, and the ISD is required to do so if it receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of the combined membership as of the most recent membership count date.

Two further recitals supply the policy argument. The intermediate school districts in both Wayne and Macomb County are currently authorized to levy a voter-approved regional enhancement millage, which the resolution says provides greater student opportunities that may include but are not limited to reduced class sizes, enhanced program offerings, improved school safety, and increased staff retention and attraction — benefits that Oakland County currently does not receive. The resolution then states that Oakland County residents deserve the opportunity to provide competitive educational opportunities and similar resources to those available in neighboring Wayne and Macomb counties, and that voters should have the ability to determine whether to support these efforts.

The operative section contains five numbered resolutions. First, the School District requests that Oakland Schools submit to its electors the question of a regional enhancement millage proposal for 1.50 mills for a period of six years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, at the school election to be held on August 4, 2026, pursuant to a ballot proposal substantially in the form attached as Exhibit A. Second, the District approves the ballot wording substantially in the form attached, subject to revision and finalization by Oakland Schools as necessary. Third, the Superintendent is authorized and directed to deliver a certified copy of the resolution to the Secretary of the Board of Education of Oakland Schools. Fourth, the resolution is expressly only a request: the proposal will be submitted to voters only if Oakland Schools receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of the combined membership of its constituent districts on or before March 31, 2026. Fifth, conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

Exhibit A contains the ballot language itself, captioned "OAKLAND SCHOOLS INTERMEDIATE SCHOOL DISTRICT, STATE OF MICHIGAN — REGIONAL ENHANCEMENT MILLAGE PROPOSAL." It opens by stating that revenue raised will be collected by Oakland Schools ISD and distributed on an equal per-pupil basis to local public school districts and eligible public school academies within the ISD's boundaries. The question asks whether the limitation on ad valorem taxes on taxable property in the Oakland Schools ISD may be increased by 1.5 mills ($1.50 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation) for six years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, as new additional millage to provide funds to enhance other state and local funding for public school operating purposes. The ballot states the millage would raise an estimated $125,756,247 if approved and first levied in 2026, and provides YES and NO options. The exhibit then begins listing the school districts and public school academies within Oakland Schools' boundaries eligible to receive the revenue.

The document follows the standard Michigan template with blank PRESENT/ABSENT member lines, blank mover and supporter lines, blank AYES and NAYS, a "RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED" line, and the Secretary's certification of compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Oakland County School Boards Association proposed bylaws amendments for 2026, presented to member districts for consideration. Amendment 1 would let the Intermediate School District, which pays $6,000 in annual dues directly to the Association, appoint one Trustee to a three-year term on the nine-member Board of Directors. Amendment 2 would require that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee be a member of the Board of Directors.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A two-page OCSBA (Oakland County School Boards Association) document titled "PROPOSED BYLAWS UPDATES FOR 2026," circulated to member districts for consideration in spring 2026.

Proposed Amendment 1 — ISD appointment to the Board of Directors
Adds language to Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility): the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the Association and is therefore entitled to appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors. If the ISD declines, it must notify the Board in writing within 30 days of a Board election so the seat can be filled by election.

Rationale: the ISD is the only member district that also pays annual dues directly to the Association, currently $6,000 per year. The Board of Directors is a working board and it is a struggle to fill all 9 positions, so the appointment provides continuity and consistently fills one seat without altering the total number of Directors or the one-director-per-district limit. The document cites the ISD's in-kind support: event space with AV equipment and staff, legislative affairs and advocacy support, and employee speakers at no cost. ISD dues cover the entire cost the Association pays the ISD for event management and financial services agreements.

Proposed Amendment 2 — committee leadership
Revises Article IX, Sections 3 and 4. Where an elected committee chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors as Vice-Chair. Applied to the Government Relations Committee, this replaces the default of the OCSBA Vice President assuming the Vice Chair role.

Rationale: assigning a Director as Vice-Chair provides board support, ensures two-way communication with the Board, and ensures compliance with board procedures and bylaws. For the GRC specifically, both Chair and Vice Chair must be actively involved in advocacy and attend state and national conferences, so the OCSBA Vice President is not always best suited.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is the Oakland County School Boards Association's "PROPOSED BYLAWS UPDATES FOR 2026," a two-page circulation to member districts. It appears in the Troy School District board packet for both the June 1 and June 16, 2026 meetings as part of the OCSBA spring member-consideration materials.

Proposed Amendment 1 would allow a member district that pays dues directly to the Association to appoint a Trustee to a seat on the Board of Directors. The amendment adds language to Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility). The existing text provides that any Member is eligible to be elected to the Board of Directors and that only one Member from each Member School District may serve at any given time. The added language provides that the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the Association and is therefore entitled to appoint one (1) Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors; if the ISD chooses not to exercise this right, the Board of Directors shall be notified in writing within 30 days of a Board election so that the seat can be filled by election.

The stated rationale is that, like every other member district, the ISD is a member of MASB and therefore of the Association, but the ISD is the only member district that also pays annual dues — currently $6,000 per year — directly to the Association. The proposal is framed as helping the Association through board continuity: the Board of Directors is described as a working board, and filling all 9 positions is a struggle, so this would consistently fill one seat. An appointment by a dues-paying district would not alter the total number of Directors, and the limit of one director per district does not change. The document further cites the ISD's unparalleled financial and in-kind support: in-kind donations of event space with AV support (equipment and staff), legislative affairs and advocacy support, and employee speakers provided at no cost when requested. The ISD's annual dues cover the entire cost the Association pays the ISD for service agreements — Event Management services including staff, online registration, collection and processing of meeting fees and onsite event support, and Financial Services support including monthly financial accounting and filing of annual tax and state reports.

The document reproduces related bylaw language for reference only, which would not change: Article III Membership Section 1, defining Members as publicly elected Board of Education members of Oakland County school districts or elected Oakland ISD Board members who are also MASB members in good standing; Article IV Dues, providing that the Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, ISD membership dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts; and Article VI Section 1, providing that the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9.

Proposed Amendment 2 would ensure that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors, by adding or revising language in two sections of Article IX.

In Article IX Section 3 (Committee Chairs), the added sentence provides that in the event the elected committee chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as Vice-Chair of the committee. The existing framework — each standing and ad hoc committee electing a Chairperson annually from appointed representatives, with the election as first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1 and at least seven calendar days' written notice — is unchanged. The rationale is that any member can be elected to chair any committee, so when a chair is not on the Board of Directors, assigning a Director as Vice-Chair provides board support, ensures direct two-way communication between committee and board, and ensures compliance with board procedures and Association bylaws.

In Article IX Section 4 (The Government Relations Committee), the revision replaces the existing default that, in the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position, with the same Director-appointment mechanism. The rationale explains that while all Directors serve on one or more committees, Directors are not necessarily involved in the GRC and some never attend its meetings, whereas the GRC Vice Chair must regularly attend. Like the GRC Chair, the Vice Chair needs to be knowledgeable and actively involved in advocacy, providing leadership by regularly attending state and national advocacy conferences and events such as MASB Behind the Scenes and the NSBA Advocacy Institute. For these reasons the OCSBA Vice President is not always best suited, and the Board of Directors should decide which Director is.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: OCSBA's proposed new resolution for spring 2026 member consideration, opposing any tying of school funding to waiver of the attorney-client privilege. The rationale cites FY26 School Aid Act section 31aa, under which districts opting in to school safety and mental health categorical funding agreed to cooperate with investigations — including waiving attorney-client privilege — following a mass-casualty incident. The document also reproduces OCSBA's full set of continuing resolutions for reference.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A three-page OCSBA circulation for spring 2026 containing one proposed new resolution plus the Association's complete continuing resolutions, provided for reference with adoption and amendment dates noted.

The proposed new resolution
"OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege."

Rationale: in the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to opt in, and any district opting in agreed to cooperate with an investigation — including waiving the attorney-client privilege — following a mass-casualty incident. The document argues that while cooperation with post-incident investigations is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, the courts have ruled on the issue, and nothing would stop the legislature from tying privilege waiver to other funding in future.

Adoption threshold
Per OCSBA Bylaws Article IX Section 5, resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association.

Continuing resolutions reproduced
Accountability and Transparency; Broadband Access and Devices; Early Childhood; Early On Michigan; Evidence-Based Decision Making; Lame Duck; Local Control; Mental Health; Non-Partisan Elections; School Aid; School Finance Research Collaborative; School Nutrition; School Safety; Special Education; Teacher Shortages; Unfunded Mandates. Most cite corresponding MASB resolution numbers.

Notable positions
School Aid asks that the School Aid Fund be constitutionally limited to Pre-K–12 public education and opposes vouchers or tax credit programs; supports additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students; and supports enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1. Special Education supports full funding of IDEA, noting federal appropriations have fallen short of the promised 40 percent of excess cost.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This three-page OCSBA document, headed "Proposed NEW Resolution May, 2026," was circulated to member school districts for spring 2026 consideration and appears in the Troy School District packets for both June 1 and June 16, 2026.

The proposed new resolution is a single sentence: "OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege."

The rationale explains the trigger. In the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in," and any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation — including waiving the attorney-client privilege — following a mass-casualty incident. The document argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on this issue, and that in future there is nothing to stop the legislature from tying waiver of the attorney-client privilege to other funding.

The balance of the document reproduces OCSBA's continuing resolutions, provided for reference only, with adoption and amendment dates noted for each. The document cites OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 on Resolution Adoption: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

The continuing resolutions are:

Accountability and Transparency (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025) — supports holding every school receiving public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities.

Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025) — broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; supports funding to expand affordable reliable broadband, federal and state programs for internet-capable devices and software, and dedicated cybersecurity resources.

Early Childhood (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025) — supports additional new dollars for universal public preschool for all four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-olds.

Early On Michigan (adopted 1/26/2026) — supports full funding of Early On Michigan, the early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at risk of delay.

Evidence-Based Decision Making (adopted 9/24/2019) — supports evidence-based education policy maximizing opportunities for highest achievement.

Lame Duck (adopted 9/24/2019) — supports lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

Local Control (adopted 9/24/2019) — supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards.

Mental Health (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025) — supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools with at minimum annual inflation-adjusted state resources; helping staff identify potential student mental health issues; and encouraging MDE to develop a model policy for identification and staff response.

Non-Partisan Elections (adopted 1/9/2026) — supports non-partisan school board elections.

School Aid (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025) — four parts: (A) specify in Michigan's Constitution that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education and oppose private school vouchers or tax credit programs; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes; (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts have factual information to meet their constitutional and statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30.

School Finance Research Collaborative (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025) — supports implementing SFRC recommendations while holding higher funded districts harmless.

School Nutrition (adopted 3/3/2023; amended 6/5/2025) — supports codification of free universal meals.

School Safety (adopted 3/3/2023) — supports adequate state resources to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

Special Education (adopted 9/24/2019) — supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, noting federal legislation initially promised 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities but appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local districts to make up the difference.

Teacher Shortages (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025) — supports statewide initiatives to address shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality preparation programs, including incentives to enter and complete teaching programs, incentives to remain in the classroom, and easing Michigan certification for out-of-state certified teachers.

Unfunded Mandates (adopted 9/24/2019) — opposes state or federal legislation increasing district costs without full funding.

A final clause provides that when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the legislative agendas of NSBA, MASB, the Oakland County Superintendents Association, and COSSBA.

What it is
The MHSAA reference packet "High School Cooperative Agreement — Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," filed with Troy's 2026-27 boys lacrosse cooperative request.

Enrollment thresholds
Section 1(E) sets a 1,000-student baseline. Section 1(E)(2) allows the Executive Committee to exceed any enrollment maximum for two or more schools of the same public school district in named sports including boys lacrosse — but requires a demonstrated history of low participation and states it "will not be approved based on financial concerns." Section 1(F)(1) caps combined enrollment at 3,500 for boys lacrosse; 1(F)(2) at 5,500 for ice hockey; 1(F)(3) and (4) allow four-year exceptions for newly sponsored or previously dropped sports.

Procedures
Application on MHSAA forms by the cooperating schools' administrations, accompanied by a resolution of authorization from each board of education describing the purpose and indicating which district oversees administration locally, plus a resolution of support from each league — or from four future opponents if there is no league. One school is designated primary host and becomes the official team name.

Approval criteria
Lack of numbers of students to support a program; lack of qualified staff to coach; lack of facilities; and evidence of a desire to increase participation opportunities in new programs — explicitly "not win/loss records of existing programs."

The adverse note
"The MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than continue to renew cooperative programs over a period of years without careful evaluation."

Advance preparation
Schools are asked to settle in writing who pays for uniforms, travel, coaches, facilities and insurance; whose training rules, academic regulations, identity, mascot and colors apply; how gate receipts are handled; and whether an existing program's students would be displaced. A Cooperative Program Board of Control is recommended.

It contains four parts: Handbook Regulation I Section 1 with interpretations, the application procedures, advance preparation material, and the blank senior high application form.

Section 1(E) provides that in any sport, two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 1,000 students may conduct a Cooperative Program with Executive Committee approval. Subsection 1(E)(1) permits subvarsity-only cooperatives regardless of enrollment, requiring a demonstrated history of inadequate participation and stating they will not be approved based on financial concerns; students retain varsity eligibility only at their school of actual enrollment, and the deadlines and two-year minimum do not apply. Subsection 1(E)(2) — the provision most relevant to Troy — permits the Executive Committee to approve a cooperative regardless of the combined enrollment maximum in named sports including boys and girls lacrosse, for two or more schools of the same public school district sharing a governing board. It again requires a demonstrated history of low participation numbers and states the program will not be approved based on financial concerns, does not apply to public school academies, is decided case by case, requires league or conference approval, and is subject to the standard deadlines.

Section 1(F)(1) permits combined enrollment up to 3,500 students in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools: field hockey, gymnastics, boys and girls lacrosse, boys and girls alpine skiing, boys and girls swimming and diving, boys and girls tennis, and boys volleyball. Section 1(F)(2) sets 5,500 for ice hockey. Section 1(F)(3) allows the Executive Committee to waive the 3,500 or 5,500 maximum where none of the schools sponsored the sport at any level in the previous year, but the agreement may not exist beyond four school years. Section 1(F)(4) allows exceeding the maximum for up to four years where, in the previous year, the school or its cooperative dropped the sport for demonstrated lack of participation.

The interpretations govern duration and consequences. Cooperative programs run a minimum of two years but may be voided at any time by resolution of any cooperating board; termination before the second year bars the terminating school from another cooperative in those sports for two years. Dissolution deadlines are May 1 for fall sports, August 15 for winter and October 15 for spring. Agreements under Section 1(E) whose enrollment later exceeds 1,000, as established each February, dissolve before the affected school year. If combined enrollment exceeds the original Division in the second year, the schools play in the higher MHSAA tournament Division. A new member school otherwise ineligible for tournaments may participate sooner by joining a cooperative with a tournament-eligible school. Failure to submit the MHSAA Membership Resolution by the fourth Friday after Labor Day bars that school's students from all MHSAA tournaments. Agreements including a Class A or B school, or three or more schools, must submit a renewal form every two years prior to May 1, requiring league approval plus participation and win/loss statistics; agreements between only two Class C or D schools need no renewal. A league may void an agreement at renewal by vote, with notification before April 1. Adding schools requires a new application. Programs started under Section 1(F) over the 3,500 limit complete the two-year renewal process and dissolve automatically after the fourth year. Cooperative programs in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools are classified by the combined enrollment of the cooperating schools, and programs whose February Enrollment Declaration exceeds the applicable limit may not operate the coming year. Deadlines for newly forming cooperatives are May 1, August 15 and October 15 by season.

The procedures section requires application on MHSAA forms by the administrations of the cooperating member schools, received even if partially completed by the deadline. The application must be accompanied by a resolution of authorization from each cooperating board of education describing the purpose for sponsoring the program and the advance preparation materials, and indicating which school or district is responsible for overseeing administration locally; plus a resolution of support from each league or conference, or from at least four future opponents where there is no league. One school must be designated primary host and is considered the official team name, with all signatures and enrollment figures from the most recent Enrollment Declaration Form. Applications go to the Executive Committee, which considers lack of numbers of students to support a program, lack of qualified staff to coach, lack of facilities, and evidence of a desire to increase opportunities for participation in new programs — explicitly not the win/loss records of existing programs. Agreements are effective for two years, and no other cooperative in the same sports may be made until that period lapses.

A note carrying particular weight for two large Troy high schools states: "The MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than continue to renew cooperative programs over a period of years without careful evaluation. Schools should review participation numbers annually and consider the feasibility of separate teams in order to maximize opportunities for students at each school involved in the cooperative program."

The advance preparation material poses questions schools should settle before applying: whether students from another school would replace local students and deny local taxpayers' children the opportunity to participate; who pays for and maintains uniforms, equipment and facilities; who pays for travel to practices and contests; who selects, supervises and pays coaches; whose cheerleaders cheer; whose training rules and letter award guidelines apply; whose academic and other regulations apply; whether daily class schedules can be coordinated; how gate receipts are handled; where practices and games are held and who pays; who hosts and supervises events; whether athletic accident insurance is provided and who pays, and whether liability insurers have been notified; whose school identity, mascot and colors are used; and whether an existing sport would suffer from creating a cooperative in another sport that season.

The guidelines recommend addressing all issues in writing in advance and submitting them with the application, since many schools have later sought a written historical record; appointing a "Cooperative Program Board of Control" of at least an administrator and athletic director from each school to initiate the program and resolve disputes; keeping cooperating districts adjacent with reasonable travel distance; seeking cooperatives only in sports where opportunities are limited and students are not expected to be cut; and treating agreements as intended for a significant group of students over several years rather than one or two participants. It cautions that programs comprising several schools tend to resemble non-school sports and may blur the philosophy of school sports.

The packet closes with the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team, including the checkbox list of the regulation under which the agreement is formed, team levels to be sponsored, prior sponsorship disclosure, the two-year minimum acknowledgment, league support attachment, team naming, and the Cooperative Program Board of Control signature blocks requiring superintendent, board of education, principal and athletic director signatures from each school. Completed forms are emailed to coops@mhsaa.com.

What it is
The full OCSBA bylaws document circulated for spring 2026 member consideration, with the proposed amendments embedded in context. Adopted by the Board of Directors 11/15/2017; by general membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; amended by member school districts 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021, 3/3/2023 and 6/6/2025. Principal office: 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township.

The embedded amendments (pages 4, 8, 9)
- Article VI Section 2 — the ISD, which pays annual dues directly, may appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors; if it declines it must notify the Board in writing within 30 days of an election
- Article IX Sections 3 and 4 — where an elected committee chair is not a Director, the Association Board appoints one of its Directors as Vice-Chair, replacing the default that the OCSBA Vice President fills that role on the Government Relations Committee

Governance essentials
- Membership: any elected Oakland County or Oakland ISD board member whose district is in good standing with MASB
- Voting: one vote per Member, but one vote per Member School District on resolutions and bylaws amendments
- Quorum: at least one Member from 25% of Member School Districts
- Board of Directors: odd number, 7 to 9, three-year terms, one Member per district, elected each June; three consecutive absences constitute resignation
- Officers: President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer, elected from the Board
- Committees: Government Relations (meets at least 6 times a year) and Resolutions and Bylaws (at least once)
- Resolutions become Association policy at 19 member districts
- Bylaws amendments: written ballot, at least a 40-day voting window, one vote per district

Finance
Expenditures over $2,500 require Board approval plus both President and Treasurer signatures; up to $2,500 either officer may approve. The Treasurer reports quarterly, presents a budget by the June meeting and year-end reports by August 30. An external audit is conducted only if required by law or a third party. The Board may contract Oakland Schools for administrative and financial services.

This document is the complete bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association as circulated to member districts in spring 2026, with the proposed amendments shown in place — a cover note directs readers to pages 4, 8 and 9. The adoption history is recorded on the first page: adopted by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017, by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018, with amendments approved by member school districts on 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021, 3/3/2023 and 6/6/2025.

Article I locates the principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County, and requires a continuously maintained registered office and agent.

Article II sets out eight purposes: advancing the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards; promoting high standards in educational programs and services for all students; making information on educational issues available to board members; conducting and sponsoring meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; promoting public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; enhancing cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards; presenting a strong force representing school board views to political representatives; and advocating for county, state and national legislation supporting public education by locally elected boards.

Article III defines membership as any publicly elected board member of an Oakland County school district, or any elected Oakland ISD board member, whose district is also a member in good standing of MASB. Each Member has one vote on matters submitted to the Members, exercised in person, with two exceptions: each Member School District has one vote on resolutions under Article IX and on bylaws amendments under Article XVI, recorded on receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of that district's trustees, and results are reported to all districts by the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting is granted to the Board of Directors only for emergency business, reaffirmed at its next meeting. Membership is not transferable.

Article IV provides that the Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association members, Intermediate School District membership dues not exceeding that grant, and contributions and gifts.

Article V requires an annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings each year, the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings may be called by the President or two Directors with 30 days' notice. Written notice is delivered personally or by email not less than ten nor more than fifty days before a meeting. Quorum is the presence of at least one Member from twenty-five percent of the Member School Districts. Superintendents and administrators are encouraged to participate.

Article VI governs the Board of Directors. Section 1 requires an odd number, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with the Board having discretion to set the number, considering a change whenever an election produces fewer candidates than open seats; decreases are accomplished by attrition, which may leave an eight-member Board for up to a year. Section 2 makes any Member eligible, with only one Member per district serving at a time, and carries the first proposed amendment: the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the Association and is therefore entitled to appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term, and if it declines must notify the Board in writing within 30 days of a Board election so the seat can be filled by election. Section 3 sets three-year terms. Section 4 requires an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors convened by May 1, seeking candidates giving geographical balance across Oakland County, with applications sent to all districts, no nominations from the floor, and election at the June meeting by written ballot where candidates exceed vacancies. Section 5 allows resignation by written notice and removal with cause as defined in Appendix I by majority vote. Section 6 governs vacancies. Section 7 provides that failure to attend three consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation absent an excused absence requested in writing within thirty days.

Article VII covers Board meetings, notice, a majority quorum, action by majority of Directors serving, no stated salaries, informal action by unanimous written consent, confidentiality of Board proceedings absent advance authorization, and a requirement to maintain Board Operating Procedures.

Article VIII establishes the offices of President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer, elected from the current Board. The President is Chief Executive Officer with general and active management. The Secretary attends all meetings and records votes and minutes, and the office may be divided into Corresponding and Recording Secretary roles. The Treasurer has custody of funds, keeps accounts, deposits monies, disburses as ordered, and reports at regular meetings, and may be required to furnish a bond.

Article IX governs committees. Quorum is twenty-five percent of appointed representatives, with alternates counted only when the primary is absent. Section 3 carries the second proposed amendment: each committee elects a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives, and where the elected chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as Vice-Chair. Section 4 establishes the Government Relations Committee as a standing committee meeting at least six times per year to receive and share legislative information, electing its chair annually after January 31, with the same Director-as-Vice-Chair amendment replacing the prior default that the OCSBA Vice President assumes that role; it reviews and revises Legislative Priorities annually for Board approval. Section 5 establishes the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, meeting at least once per year, appointed by the President, including the Government Relations Committee Chair. Resolutions or bylaws revisions may be initiated by a member district board, the Board of Directors, or either committee; the Board reviews all proposals before submission to member districts, which vote at their next meeting within a window of at least forty calendar days. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen Member School Districts become the official position of the Association.

Article X governs dissolution and prohibits inurement of net earnings under Section 501(c)(4). Article XI covers fiduciary and financial responsibilities: expenditures may not exceed the approved annual budget; no committee may create financial liability without majority Member authorization; expenditures exceeding $2,500 require Board approval and both President and Treasurer signatures, while expenditures up to $2,500 may be approved by either, with the Vice-President substituting in their absence. The Treasurer distributes reports quarterly, presents a budget for the upcoming fiscal year no later than the June Board meeting and end-of-year revenue and expense reports no later than August 30, with the approved budget and annual report presented at the first fall Member Meeting. Annually the Association performs agreed-upon procedures on its financial records; an external audit is conducted only if required by law or a third party. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools, monitored by the Treasurer.

Article XII provides extensive indemnification of directors, officers, employees and agents to the fullest extent permitted by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act, covering third-party claims and claims brought by or in the right of the Association, with provisions on actions brought by the indemnitee, approval procedures, advancement of expenses, partial indemnification, other rights, liability insurance, severability and definitions.

Article XIII leaves the fiscal year to the Board. Article XIV addresses conflicts of interest, requiring officers, directors, committee members and employees to avoid conflicts, disclose interests, refrain from voting or exerting influence, and be excluded from quorum determination on affected matters, with minutes reflecting the disclosure, abstention and quorum situation. Article XV covers contracts, execution of instruments, borrowing, adjourned meetings, notice by electronic communication to district-provided email, action by written consent, remote participation by two-way communication counting as presence, and the corporate seal.

Article XVI provides that the bylaws may be altered or amended by vote of the Member School Districts, with the Board providing a written ballot and at least a forty-day voting period, one vote per district; grammatical corrections not changing meaning may be made by the Board without a vote. It also permits the Board to adopt additional rules and regulations, and to set aside rules during a declared local, state or national emergency.

Appendix 1, adopted by the Board of Directors on September 16, 2020, defines cause for removing a board member or officer. It prefaces the definition with the three primary legal duties of a nonprofit board — the duty of care, duty of loyalty and duty of obedience — and lists as cause: acts of malfeasance, misfeasance or nonfeasance; willful failure to follow OCSBA bylaws; willful neglect of duties; failure to disclose a conflict of interest or using the Association for personal gain; using the position or the OCSBA logo in a political endorsement; frequently missed board or committee meetings; creating an unhealthy or dysfunctional boardroom through inappropriate behavior or disrespect; and ethical concerns such as discrimination, harassment or criminal behavior. It closes by noting removal should only be done when absolutely necessary.

What it is
The spring 2026 revision of the Troy School District Athletic Handbook for Student-Athletes, presented as agenda item 3C in April 2026. It integrates MHSAA rules as adopted by the district with district-specific policies, operates under the umbrella of the Student Code of Conduct, and is in effect year-round.

Eligibility (Section I)
Enrollment by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester; under 19 for grades 9-12, under 14 and 15 for grades 7 and 8. All registration through FinalForms — parent and student accounts, electronic forms, a physical dated on or after April 15 of the previous school year, and health history — completed before any tryout, practice or competition. Paper submissions are no longer accepted. Four seasons per sport across grades 9-12; four first and four second semesters of eligibility.

Academic standards
Pass five of six classes the previous semester as the district standard. Troy College and Career High School and International Academy require seven of eight; Intersect and Inspire five of six; middle school five of six per quarter. Eligibility is reviewed each marking period; a student may regain it with a weekly progress report, with ineligibility no less than one full calendar week. Deficiencies from a prior semester carry a minimum sixty scheduled school days. New transfers get one transitional semester at the MHSAA minimum of four classes.

Conduct and discipline
Awards capped at $25 fair market value. Amateur status required. Outside-of-school competition in the same sport during the season brings a minimum two-contest (middle school) or three-contest (high school) penalty. Substance violations are cumulative across a high school career and escalate from one contest to permanent loss of eligibility at a fourth alcohol/drug violation. Section XIV sets four violation levels with suspensions of 0%, 10-20%, 20-40% and 50-100% of the season.

NIL / Personal Branding
Permitted under MHSAA rules provided activities are independent of school teams, compensation is not tied to performance or participation, and no school names, logos, uniforms or facilities are used. Collectives and group agreements are prohibited.

This is the draft Troy School District Athletic Handbook for Students, revised spring 2026 and presented to the Board of Education as agenda item 3C at the April 7 and April 21, 2026 meetings. Its introduction describes it as a consistent framework of expectations for all student-athletes regardless of team or school, integrating MHSAA rules as adopted by the district with district-specific policies. Athletics are framed as a vital extension of the classroom developing social-emotional learning, personal responsibility, teamwork, leadership, time management and athletic skill. The handbook operates under the umbrella of the Student Code of Conduct — a violation of the Code is also subject to handbook discipline — and is in effect throughout the entire year. Policies marked with an asterisk are district-adopted policies that also align with MHSAA regulations.

Section I sets the rules of eligibility. Students must be enrolled by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester in which they compete, reside in the boundaries of the school they attend, and compete for that school; students attending TCCHS and IA East must participate at their home school based on residency. Age limits are under nineteen for grades nine through twelve and under fourteen and fifteen for seventh and eighth grade respectively, with a birthday on or after September 1 preserving eligibility for the balance of the year. All registration runs through FinalForms, the district's designated digital platform for athletic clearance, requiring completed parent and student accounts, all electronic forms and agreements, a current physical uploaded and dated after April 15 of the previous school year, and a completed health history and medical profile — all approved before any tryouts, practices or competitions. Families must read and acknowledge the Athletic Handbook, the CAP PACT Agreement, the Application to Participate, the Pay to Participate Agreement (paid before the first competition), the Athletics Transportation Agreement, the Concussion Awareness form and the MHSAA Acknowledgement of Risk. Paper submissions are no longer accepted.

The physical examination must be completed by a physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner and submitted electronically. Students may have no more than four seasons of competition in a sport across grades 9-12, distributed across no more than four first and four second semesters, and no more than one season per sport per school year even where a sport is offered twice; fall sideline cheer does not count as a competition season alongside winter competitive cheer. Grades 7 and 8 are not limited in seasons or semesters, but once a student enters ninth grade semesters must be consecutive.

Academic eligibility requires passing grades in a minimum of five classes the previous semester as the combined MHSAA and district standard, with variations by school: Troy College and Career High School students must pass seven of eight classes over the previous two semesters; Intersect and Inspire High School students five of six over the previous two semesters; International Academy seven of eight in the previous semester; and middle school students five of six in the previous quarter. A student ineligible on previous-semester final grades is ineligible for the complete following semester unless eligible under the 60-Day Rule. Eligibility is formally reviewed at the end of each marking period, every ten weeks, and a student falling short becomes ineligible for competition but may regain eligibility by submitting a weekly academic progress report, with ineligibility lasting no less than one full calendar week Monday through Sunday.
